en.html:
There had not been many occasions for me to use a railway.

Where I grew up was countryside in the literal sense: no station, no tracks. Later, after conscription, I did ride a train on military service, but even that amounted to only a few occasions.
After demobilization, when I had returned home and taken a job, another two or three.

Had Rokuhara not restricted civilian rail travel after taking power, there might have been a few more. ...Though nobody at the company considered me suitable for outside work, and for <ruby>private<rt>private</rt></ruby> pleasure I had no habit of traveling. A few more, not very many.

Such was my railway experience: one hand would do for counting it. The speed, the inside of the carriage, the scenery flowing past the window—none had become familiar enough to lose its novelty.

過去、鉄道を利用する機会は少なかった。

　育った土地は文字通りの片田舎で駅も線路もなく、
長じて徴兵を受け軍役に就いた折には汽車に乗ること
もあったが、それとてせいぜい数度ばかり。
　復員して郷里に戻り、就職してからほんの二、三度。

　六波羅が政権掌握後に民間人の鉄道利用を規制して
いなければ、もう少し回数は増えていたろう。
　……会社では俺を外勤向きと評価する人などおらず、
<ruby>私<rt>し</rt></ruby>で旅行する趣味もなかったから、高は知れているが。

　そんな次第で、俺は片手で数えて足りる程度にしか
鉄道の旅の経験がない。
　この速さも、内装も、窓の外を流れる風景も、まだ
慣れず、斬新な印象の残るものだった。

en.html:
Sayo"You are not quite settled, I see."
Kageaki"I am ashamed to admit it. A little."
Sayo"Only a little patience is required, sir."
Kageaki"It is not discomfort. Please do not trouble yourself. ...You, Chamberlain, seem quite untroubled."
Sayo"Every wrinkle has its experience behind it. In particular, when I was living in Europe with my lady, we were taking trains as a matter of daily routine."
Kageaki"I hear electrically powered trains have become common there."
Sayo"Yes, that is so. For short routes within the cities, I should think they are already the main kind. Between cities, steam locomotives are still very much in the majority..."
Sayo"Though in some places, it seems, they are using electric locomotives also."
Kageaki"? Are those different from electrically powered trains?"
Sayo"What you have in mind, Mr. Minato, would be the arrangement where each carriage has its own power. There is also the other arrangement: an electric locomotive does the pulling, and the other carriages follow."
Kageaki"Ah... I see. In short, the usual steam locomotive, only made electric?"
Sayo"Quite correct. But Mr. Minato, please do not let that observation out too carelessly. Once certain railway enthusiastsmaniacs get hold of it—"
Sayo"You may be given a thorough lecture lasting, by my estimate, forty-two hours. Beginning with how both systems originated, then the machinery in detail, every small point of difference, how they are actually operated, and finally their prospects for the future."
Kageaki"? ...Yes."

Kageaki"...Even so. We were allowed aboard with very little difficulty."
Sayo"They say the trains going out of Aizu are packed with wealthy people who wish to leave before the war starts. A civilian wanting to go the other way, toward central Aizu, must have rather exceptional tastes."
Sayo"As far as seats are concerned, take your pick. Provided, of course, you can pay fares that are absurdly high compared with Europe."
Kageaki"Yes. That is one matter, but what I was concerned about is another. Aizu at present is as good as under martial law—"
Kageaki"I thought the army would have requisitioned every train. Or, even if it had left room for civilian use, surely they would be making strict checks before allowing us aboard."

Kageaki"And once we have got aboard, it is the fastest and most efficient means of travel..."
Sayo"Sit and wait; you arrive. Our one concern, perhaps, is that if trouble should occur on board, getting away becomes difficult."
Kageaki"There is a risk of such trouble?"
Sayo"We cannot say there is none. In another carriage, a company of the Sasagawa army is sharing our train."
Kageaki"...That might make matters rather awkward, should we come face to face."
Sayo"There is that possibility. ...But these are reservists called back to service."
Sayo"Their assignment appears to be logistics, and their morale and equipment seem no more than that calls for. Careless we must not become, but there is no occasion for great anxiety."

en.html:
Captain Ootori was looking at the scenery.
No—that was not quite correct.

She had the <ruby>air<rt>air</rt></ruby> of someone whose mind was elsewhere. Her gaze was turned toward the view, but fixed at one angle, <ruby>hardly<rt>hardly</rt></ruby> responding as the landscape changed.

Not outside, but inside herself? Was that where those narrow eyes were looking now? If so, what did they see?
What feelings in this woman, Kanae Ootori—

Perhaps I had started entertaining such uncharacteristic, prying questions because the sight of her deep in thought had drawn me in.
Unlike the Captain I usually saw, for some reason she now looked like a woman in the ordinary sense of the word.
Fleeting, vulnerable. <ruby>Delicate<rt>delicate</rt></ruby> and faint.

She resembled the woman I had <ruby>once<rt>once</rt></ruby> seen playing the <ruby>stringed instrument<rt>double bass</rt></ruby>.
Resembled her, yes—but there was a difference. That time, she had possessed a definite intention. It had led the notes and made them into <ruby>music<rt>music</rt></ruby>. Now, something of that intention was missing from her <ruby>countenance<rt>face</rt></ruby>.

Like a lost child who could no longer find the way home.

Standing all alone in a foreign place, with nothing to turn to.

Captain Ootori was looking at the scenery.
No—that was not quite correct.

She had the airair of someone whose mind was elsewhere. Her gaze was turned toward the view, but fixed at one angle, hardlyhardly responding as the landscape changed.

Not outside, but inside herself? Was that where those narrow eyes were looking now? If so, what did they see?
What feelings in this woman, Kanae Ootori—

Perhaps I had started entertaining such uncharacteristic, prying questions because the sight of her deep in thought had drawn me in.
Unlike the Captain I usually saw, for some reason she now looked like a woman in the ordinary sense of the word.
Fleeting, vulnerable. Delicatedelicate and faint.

She resembled the woman I had onceonce seen playing the stringed instrumentdouble bass.
Resembled her, yes—but there was a difference. That time, she had possessed a definite intention. It had led the notes and made them into musicmusic. Now, something of that intention was missing from her countenanceface.

Like a lost child who could no longer find the way home.

Standing all alone in a foreign place, with nothing to turn to.

en.html:
As though a child who had lost the way had given up, and begun trudging off with no <ruby>destination<rt>destination</rt></ruby> at all—

Captain Ootori said it like that.

Somewhere.
Surely she meant somewhere <ruby>other than straight ahead<rt>・・・・・・・・</rt></ruby>...

Abandon the scheme to storm the Sasagawa Kubo's seat and strike down Shishiku Ootori. A foolish scheme—surely it was, looked at from any objective position.
Go somewhere else.

With no purpose. Or, if one had to be chosen, to escape the fighting.
Join the crowds of people now doing just that.

Not someone of consequence. A single human being.
Know one's limits, and keep to one's place...

No longer Kanae Ootori or Kageaki Minato.
No noble pride, no responsibility to put an end to Silver Star.

Choose to be nameless, and sink into the world.

—Was that what she wanted?
Was that what Captain Ootori had said?

en.text:
With one accord, we made the promise.◆
Every one of us knew that this someday・・・ would not come.

An ordinary promise, made for the moment only.◆
Countless such promises were exchanged here and thereeverywhere in the world, then forgotten, never to be remembered again.

Light conversation. Nothing more.◆

Just now, that light conversation was more painful than I could bear.

Looking at Captain Ootori's smile, without a flawflaw, was painful.
Almost fleeing it, I let my eyes turn toward the window.

The landscape filled my sight, changing and yet the same.
And—in front of it. A shape reflected in the glassglass.

A man.
